## Assignment 5, Problem 1: scattering

- General idea is:
  - Use SWIG classes to calculate trajectories for a range of (E, b).
    - Choose 4–10 E values, interesting range is ~0.5 to 2.
    - Simulate a lot of b values, interesting range is ~0 to 2.
      - ~100 is a good number; smaller $ \Delta b$ actually leads to numerical issues here.
      - ${ \theta }_{s}(b)$ is used for the remainder of the problems, and you need to differentiate it.
      - Only plot a handful of b values, not 1000 :)
    - Use the endpoint of the trajectories as ${ \theta }_{s}$ (assuming $r$ is large at the end, this is good enough).
    - Note: L–J has much more interesting behavior.
  - Use e.g. 5-point stencil function for $d{ \theta }_{s}/db$ (remember, we have ${ \theta }_{s}(b)$ calculated at a discrete set of $b$ values; think about how to define the derivative here).

## Boundary value problems

- So far, we've covered "unbounded" ODE problems: specify starting point, let system evolve.
- Boundary value problems impose an extra requirement: specific values of the state (${y}_{i}(t)$) at more than one $t$.
  - Related topic: eigenvalue problems.
- Key complication: (obviously) meeting the boundary condition is not trivial!
  - Non-local condition; our "marching" methods are intrinsically local.
  - Methods like RK4 are not always the most accurate.
- These are like "1D partial differential equations": a warmup for the real PDE section of the class.
- Reference: Numerical Recipes, Chapter 18

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

---

## Boundary value problems

- Example problem: consider a 2nd order ODE,

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{x}^{2}}=f(x,u,{u}^{′}),{u}^{′}(x)=\frac{du}{dx}$$

- The values of the state ($u(x)$ and/or ${u}^{′}(x)$) are specified on two boundaries, left (${x}_{l}$) and right $({x}_{r})$.
- We want solutions inside this interval, ${x}_{l} \leq x \leq {x}_{r}$.
- There are numerous possible scenarios:
  - Dirichlet: specify $u(x)$ on boundaries.
  - Neumann: specify ${u}^{′}(x)$ on boundaries.
  - Periodic: require $u({x}_{l})=u({x}_{r})$ and ${u}^{′}({x}_{l})={u}^{′}({x}_{r})$.
  - Or mixed, combining any of these; or partial, only specifying some variables.

## Schroedinger equation

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- A concrete example: the time-independent Schroedinger equation,

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\frac{{d}^{2} \psi }{d{x}^{2}}=-\frac{2m}{{ \hbar }^{2}}\left[ E-V(x) \right] \psi (x)$$

- Let $V(x)$ be an infinite potential well.
- This imposes Dirichlet boundary conditions:

- $$\begin{aligned}
 \psi (0)=0 \\
 \psi (L)=0
\end{aligned}$$

![](../assets/05_bvps/slide07_image1.png){fig-alt="Diagram of an infinite square well potential: V = infinity at the walls x=0 and x=L (shaded regions), V=0 in the interior between them."}

---

## Schroedinger equation

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- Of course, we can solve this problem analytically:

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\frac{{d}^{2} \psi }{d{x}^{2}}=-\frac{2m}{{ \hbar }^{2}}E \psi (x)$$

- Free particle inside the well, with solutions like:

- $$\begin{matrix}
 \psi (x) & =A{e}^{ikx}+B{e}^{-ikx}
\end{matrix}$$

![](../assets/05_bvps/slide08_image1.png){fig-alt="Diagram of an infinite square well potential: V = infinity at the walls x=0 and x=L (shaded regions), V=0 in the interior between them."}

- Apply the boundary conditions:

- $$\begin{matrix}
0= \psi (0) & =A+B \\
0= \psi (L) & =2AsinkL \\
 \Rightarrow k & =\frac{n \pi }{L}
\end{matrix}$$

---

## Schroedinger equation

- Finally, solve for the normalization, $A$:

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\begin{matrix}
1 & ={ \int }_{0}^{L}dx4{A}^{2}{sin}^{2}\left( \frac{n \pi x}{L} \right) \\
 & =4{A}^{2}\left( \frac{x}{2}-\frac{sin(n \pi x/L)}{4n \pi /L} \right){|}_{0}^{L} \\
 \Rightarrow A & =\sqrt{2/L}
\end{matrix}$$

- So, our solutions are $\begin{matrix}
 \psi (x) & =\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}sin\left( \frac{n \pi x}{L} \right)
\end{matrix}$
- And, plugging back into the original Schroedinger equation, $E= \hbar  \omega =\frac{{ \hbar }^{2}{k}^{2}}{2m}$

## Numerical BVP solving

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Two general strategies for numerical BVP algorithms:
  - Shoot:
    - Guess the solution at the left boundary.
    - "Shoot" to the right boundary, i.e., numerically solve the ODE, and see how close we are.
    - Correct the guess iteratively.

## Numerical BVP solving

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Two general strategies for numerical BVP algorithms:
  - Shoot:
    - Guess the solution at the left boundary.
    - "Shoot" to the right boundary, i.e., numerically solve the ODE, and see how close we are.
    - Correct the guess iteratively.
  - Relax:
    - Guess an initial solution on a mesh of points across the whole interval (independent of the ODE).
    - Check points on the interior; correct to satisfy the finite difference equations corresponding to the ODE.

## Shooting algorithm

- Iterative shooting procedure:
  - Guess unknown initial parameter at left side.
  - Generate trial solution with a “marching” algorithm.
  - Compute difference at boundary.
  - Iterate until difference is small.
- The key step is the iterative correction.
  - Use a root-finding method!

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

![shoot.png](../assets/05_bvps/shoot.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram illustrating the shooting method: three trial trajectories (1, 2, 3) starting from the required boundary value on the left, arcing toward the right edge - trajectory 1 overshoots and trajectory 2 undershoots the desired boundary value, while trajectory 3 (a linear combination) hits it."}

---

## Shooting algorithm

- Specifically: say we have $N$ coupled 1st ODEs
  - BVs: ${n}_{1}$ fixed on left, ${n}_{2}=N-{n}_{1}$ fixed on right.
  - On left, we can freely guess ${n}_{2}$ values, $\mathbf{v}=({v}_{0},{v}_{1},...,{v}_{{n}_{2}-1})$.
  - On right, we have ${n}_{2}$ equations from the BV requirement.
- So, we have a ${n}_{2}$-dimensional root-finding problem:
  - Minimize discrepancies between ${y}_{j}({x}_{r},\mathbf{v})$ and the BVs, as a function of $\mathbf{v}$=free parameters.

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

![shoot.png](../assets/05_bvps/shoot.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram illustrating the shooting method: three trial trajectories (1, 2, 3) starting from the required boundary value on the left, arcing toward the right edge - trajectory 1 overshoots and trajectory 2 undershoots the desired boundary value, while trajectory 3 (a linear combination) hits it."}

## Relaxing algorithm

- Relaxation algorithms work as follows:
  - Guess solution on a grid of $x$ values and the boundary.
  - Compute the derivatives with finite differences.
  - Compare the derivatives of your trial solution with the expected derivatives from the ODEs:
  - Iterate until the two agree, i.e., the difference is minimized.
- For our 2nd order ODE, this looks something like:
  - Algorithm iteratively adjust solution to obtain $G(x) \rightarrow 0$.

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$G(x)=\frac{{d}^{2}{u}_{g}}{d{x}^{2}}-f(x,{u}_{g},{u}_{g}^{′})$$

---

## Relaxing algorithm

- Specifically we use Jacobi’s relaxation algorithm:
  - Discretize the space and compute second derivatives:

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$h=\frac{1}{N},{x}_{j}=jh,{u}_{j} \equiv u({x}_{j}),j=0,1,...,N$$

- $$\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{x}^{2}}{|}_{x={x}_{j}}=\frac{{u}_{j+1}-2{u}_{j}+{u}_{j-1}}{{h}^{2}},j=1,2,...,N-1$$

- Define the difference between the trial solution, ${u}_{g,j}$, and the ODE:

- $$G({x}_{j})=\frac{{u}_{g,j+1}-2{u}_{j}+{u}_{g,j-1}}{{h}^{2}}-f({x}_{j},{u}_{g,j},{u}_{g,j}^{′}) \rightarrow 0$$

- Solve for next guess ${u}_{j}$:

- $${u}_{j} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left[ {u}_{g,j+1}+{u}_{g,i-1}+{h}^{2}f({x}_{j},{u}_{g,j},{u}_{g,j}^{′} \right]$$

---

- Specifically we use Jacobi’s relaxation algorithm:

- $$h=\frac{1}{N},{x}_{j}=jh,{u}_{j} \equiv u({x}_{j}),j=0,1,...,N$$

- $$\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{x}^{2}}{|}_{x={x}_{j}}=\frac{{u}_{j+1}-2{u}_{j}+{u}_{j-1}}{{h}^{2}},j=1,2,...,N-1$$

- Define the difference between the trial solution, ${u}_{g,j}$, and the ODE:

- $$G({x}_{j})=\frac{{u}_{g,j+1}-2{u}_{j}+{u}_{g,j-1}}{{h}^{2}}-f({x}_{j},{u}_{g,j},{u}_{g,j}^{′}) \rightarrow 0$$

- Solve for next guess ${u}_{j}$:

- $${u}_{j} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left[ {u}_{g,j+1}+{u}_{g,i-1}+{h}^{2}f({x}_{j},{u}_{g,j},{u}_{g,j}^{′} \right]$$

- Like Euler's method for ODEs, this is a "workhorse" method for more advanced algorithms

## Eigenvalue problems

- We've already seen an example of an eigenvalue problem:

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{x}^{2}}=-\frac{{ \pi }^{2}}{4}(u+1)$$

- $$u(0)=0,u(1)=1$$

- Recall back to linear algebra section: we discretize the 2nd derivative, and pack the variables into a matrix.

- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{{u}_{i-1}-2{u}_{i}+{u}_{i+1}}{{h}^{2}} & =-\frac{{ \pi }^{2}}{4}({u}_{i}+1),i=1,2,...,N-1 \\
\mathbf{M}.\mathbf{u} & =\mathbf{b}
\end{matrix}$$

---

## Eigenvalue problems

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $\mathbf{M}$ is a tridiagonal matrix:

$$\mathbf{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 2-c & -1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 2-c & -1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2-c & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 2-c & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & -1 & 2-c \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \\ u_3 \\ \vdots \\ u_{N-2} \\ u_{N-1} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} u_0+c \\ c \\ c \\ \vdots \\ c \\ u_N+c \end{pmatrix}$$

- You have already worked with this system a fair amount, so we won't belabor the point, but just note that this is all intrinsically related.

## Recap

- Introduced methods for boundary value problems: ODEs where the solution has requirements at two values of the independent variable.
- Shooting method: adjust free parameters on the left side until the BVs on the right side are satisfied.
- Relaxation method: guess solution at grid of points inside interval, and iteratively adjust until it satisfies the ODEs.
  - Works best if solutions are smooth, non-oscillatory.
  - Or if shooting methods get "trapped" by unwanted solutions.
- Next time:
  - More on BVPs and eigenvalue problems
  - Sturm–Liouville
  - Quantum harmonic oscillator
  - Periodic potential (Kronig–Penney model)

## Boundary-value and eigenvalue problems

- The $s(x)$ term makes the equation inhomogeneous.
- The Sturm–Liouville theory deals with linear homogeneous second order equations of the form:
- where p(x), r(x), w(x) are given, and lambda is a parameter, p(x) >0 and w(x) >0 in integration domain
- Need boundary conditions! Consider homogenous and linear BC’s like :

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- To continue our investigation of BVP and eigenvalue problems, consider 2nd order ODEs of the following form:

- $$\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{x}^{2}}+d(x)\frac{du}{dx}+q(x)u=s(x)$$

- $d(x),q(x),s(x)$ given

- $$-\frac{d}{dx}\left[ p(x)\frac{du}{dx} \right]+r(x)u(x)= \lambda w(x)u(x)$$

- $p(x),r(x),w(x)$ given

---

## Sturm–Liouville

- The Sturm–Liouville theory deals with linear homogeneous second order equations of the form:
- Consider "regular" scenario: over the interval $x \in [a,b]$,
  - $p(x)$, $r(x)$, $w(x)$, and ${p}^{′}(x)$ are continuous
  - $p(x)>0$ and $w(x)>0$
  - Boundary conditions of the form:

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$-\frac{d}{dx}\left[ p(x)\frac{du}{dx} \right]+r(x)u(x)= \lambda w(x)u(x)$$

- $p(x),r(x),w(x)$ given

- $ \lambda $ is a parameter

- $$\begin{matrix}
{ \alpha }_{1}u(a)+{ \alpha }_{2}{u}^{′}(a) & =0 \\
{ \beta }_{1}u(b)+{ \beta }_{2}{u}^{′}(b) & =0
\end{matrix}$$

---

## Sturm–Liouville

- Sturm–Liouville proved:
  - Nontrivial solution exist only for certain values of $ \lambda $, called eigenvalues.
  - If eigenvalues are arranged in increasing order, eigenfunctions have one additional node or zero per step.
- We can solve regular S–L problems with Numerov's method.
  - Starting point is, once again, 2nd derivative with finite differences:

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{{u}_{n+1}-2{u}_{n}+{u}_{n-1}}{{h}^{2}} & ={u}_{n}^{′′}+\frac{{h}^{2}}{12}{u}_{n}^{′′′′}+O({h}^{4})
\end{matrix}$$

- $$-\frac{d}{dx}\left[ p(x)\frac{du}{dx} \right]+r(x)u(x)= \lambda w(x)u(x)$$

## Sturm–Liouville

- Sturm–Liouville proved:
  - Nontrivial solution exist only for certain values of $ \lambda $, called eigenvalues.
  - If eigenvalues are arranged in increasing order, eigenfunctions have one additional node or zero per step.
- We can solve regular S–L problems with Numerov's method.
- Changing notation (sorry...):

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{{u}_{n+1}-2{u}_{n}+{u}_{n-1}}{{h}^{2}} & ={u}_{n}^{′′}+\frac{{h}^{2}}{12}{u}_{n}^{′′′′}+O({h}^{4})
\end{matrix}$$

- $$\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{x}^{2}}+q(x)u(x)=s(x)$$

- Starting point is, once again, 2nd derivative with finite differences:

---

## Numerov's method

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\begin{matrix}
\left( 1+\frac{{h}^{2}}{12}{q}_{n+1} \right){u}_{n+1}-2\left( 1+\frac{5{h}^{2}}{12}{q}_{n} \right){u}_{n}+\left( 1+\frac{{h}^{2}}{12}{q}_{n-1} \right){u}_{n-1} & =\frac{{h}^{2}}{12}\left( {s}_{n+1}+10{s}_{n}+{s}_{n-1} \right)+O({h}^{2})
\end{matrix}$$

- $$\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{x}^{2}}+q(x)u(x)=s(x)$$

- $$\begin{matrix}
{u}_{n}^{′′′′} & =\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{x}^{2}}\left( -q(x)u(x)+s(x) \right){|}_{x={x}_{n}} \\
 & =-\frac{{q}_{n+1}{u}_{n+1}-2{q}_{n}{u}_{n}+{q}_{n-1}{u}_{n-1}}{{h}^{2}}+\frac{{s}_{n+1}-2{s}_{n}+{s}_{n-1}}{{h}^{2}}+O({h}^{2})
\end{matrix}$$

- Write ${u}_{n}^{′′′′}$ with finite differences:

- Plug into difference equation and rearrange terms a bit...

---

## Numerov's method

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $$\begin{matrix}
\left( 1+\frac{{h}^{2}}{12}{q}_{n+1} \right){u}_{n+1}-2\left( 1+\frac{5{h}^{2}}{12}{q}_{n} \right){u}_{n}+\left( 1+\frac{{h}^{2}}{12}{q}_{n-1} \right){u}_{n-1} & =\frac{{h}^{2}}{12}\left( {s}_{n+1}+10{s}_{n}+{s}_{n-1} \right)+O({h}^{6})
\end{matrix}$$

- Numerov's method gives us a "marching" algorithm
  - Actually quite accurate! $O({h}^{6})$, even better than RK45.
  - It's a 3-point formula, so we need 2 points to start.

- Sturm–Liouville problems are common in applied mathematics.
- For example, the time-independent Schroedinger equation!

![](../assets/05_bvps/slide31_800px-HarmOsziFunktionen.png){fig-alt="Plot of the quantum harmonic oscillator eigenfunctions Psi_0(x) through Psi_7(x), each offset vertically and shown against the parabolic potential well, with increasing numbers of nodes for higher energy levels."}

- $$-\frac{{ \hbar }^{2}}{2m}\frac{{d}^{2} \psi (x)}{d{x}^{2}}+V(x) \psi (x)=E \psi (x)$$

- $$\hat{H} \psi (x)=E \psi (x)$$

- For the QHO, $\hat{H}=\frac{{\hat{p}}^{2}}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2}{\hat{x}}^{2}$

## Application: quantum harmonic oscillator

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

![](../assets/05_bvps/slide32_800px-HarmOsziFunktionen.png){fig-alt="Plot of the quantum harmonic oscillator eigenfunctions Psi_0(x) through Psi_7(x), each offset vertically and shown against the parabolic potential well, with increasing numbers of nodes for higher energy levels."}

- For the QHO, $\hat{H}=\frac{{\hat{p}}^{2}}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2}{\hat{x}}^{2}$
- You might remember the solutions from your QM class:

- $${ \psi }_{n}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{n}n!}}\left( \frac{m \omega }{ \pi  \hbar } \right){e}^{-m \omega {x}^{2}/2 \hbar } \cdot {H}_{n}\left( \sqrt{\frac{m \omega }{ \hbar }}x \right)$$

- $${H}_{n}(x)=(-1{)}^{n}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{{d}^{n}}{d{x}^{n}}\left( {e}^{-{x}^{2}} \right)$$

- $${E}_{n}= \hbar  \omega \left( n+\frac{1}{2} \right)$$

## Application: quantum harmonic oscillator

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Now, let's solve the QHO numerically.
- First, we obviously can't set the interval to $[- \infty , \infty ]$.
  - Compromise: make the interval "large enough", and just set $ \psi (-L)= \psi (L)=0$.
- Then, use Numerov's algorithm to march across the interval.
- Two caveats:
  - There are some unphysical solutions that march to infinity (mathematic property of QHO).
  - From symmetry, we want our solutions to be symmetric or antisymmetric.

- $$-\frac{{ \hbar }^{2}}{2m}\frac{{d}^{2} \psi (x)}{d{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2} \psi (x)=E \psi (x)$$

---

## Application: quantum harmonic oscillator

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Rewrite the Schroedinger equation in the Numerov method form,

- $$-\frac{{ \hbar }^{2}}{2m}\frac{{d}^{2} \psi (x)}{d{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2} \psi (x)=E \psi (x)$$

- $$\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{x}^{2}}+q(x)u(x)=s(x)$$

- $${ \psi }^{′′}+\frac{2m}{{ \hbar }^{2}}\left( E-\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2} \right) \psi (x)=0$$

- So $q(x)=\frac{2m}{{ \hbar }^{2}}\left( E(x)-\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2} \right)$

---

## Application: quantum harmonic oscillator

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- How do we ensure (anti)symmetry?
- Solution: march twice! Once from the left, once from the right.
  - Ensure that the solutions match at some $x$ value.
  - We can actually multiply one of the solutions by a constant (still solves the ODE), so specifically, we ensure:

- $${ \phi }_{left}({x}_{match})={ \phi }_{right}({x}_{match})$$

  - Then, once we have a match, we can test for continuity of the derivative:

- $$\frac{{ \phi }_{left}}{dx}{|}_{{x}_{match}}=\frac{{ \phi }_{right}}{dx}{|}_{{x}_{match}}$$

- $$-\frac{{ \hbar }^{2}}{2m}\frac{{d}^{2} \psi (x)}{d{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2} \psi (x)=E \psi (x)$$

---

## Application: quantum harmonic oscillator

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
- We can choose the matching point to be at the classical turning point, i.e., where $V(x)=\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2}=E$.
- Then, we write the matching equation as follows:
- $$0=F(E)=\frac{ \pm \left[ { \phi }_{left}({x}_{m}+h)-{ \phi }_{left}({x}_{m}-h) \right]-\left[ { \phi }_{right}({x}_{m}+h)-{ \phi }_{right}({x}_{m}-h) \right]}{2h \phi ({x}_{m})}$$
  - Finally, we use just apply root finding to $F(E)$.
    - The roots are the eigenvalues, and the corresponding $ \phi $ are the eigenfunctions.
- $$-\frac{{ \hbar }^{2}}{2m}\frac{{d}^{2} \psi (x)}{d{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}m{ \omega }^{2} \psi (x)=E \psi (x)$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![continuous.png](../assets/05_bvps/continuous.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Plot titled 'Continuous Search Function': F(E) versus E, showing a periodic sawtooth-like function with several vertical asymptotes (poles) where F(E) jumps between +10 and -10."}
:::
::::

# KRONIG–PENNEY

---

## Application: periodic potential

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Another classic problem: particle in a periodic potential.
  - Kronig–Penney model: 1D "crystal".
  - $N$ heavy nuclei at fixed lattice sites (spacing=$a)$

![](../assets/05_bvps/slide39_1d-lattice.png){fig-alt="Diagram of a 1D periodic lattice: red dots representing atoms at positions x=0, x=a, ..., x=Na along the top, with a green square-wave periodic potential V(x) drawn beneath, one well per atomic site."}

- Problem is best solved in the Fourier domain. We expect solutions like...

- $$ \psi (x)=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k}{C}_{k}{e}^{ikx}$$

- ...with periodic boundary conditions:

- $${e}^{ik(x+Na)}={e}^{ikx}$$

- $$ \Rightarrow k=\frac{2 \pi n}{Na},n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,...$$

---

## Brillouin zone

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons
- If you took solid state, you learned about the Brillouin zone ([wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brillouin_zone)):
  - For spatial lattice, the reciprocal space is the set of plane wave vectors period on the lattice
  - First Brillouin zone = points closest to origin (Voronoi cell).
- This is important because of Bloch's theorem: solutions can be completely characterized by their behavior in a single Brillouin zone.
  - This is intrinsically related to the Fourier transform and the Nyquist frequency.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Brillouin_zone.png](../assets/05_bvps/Brillouin_zone.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel diagram (a, b) showing real-space lattices of blue dots (square lattice in (a), a different symmetry in (b)) mapped by an arrow to their reciprocal-space lattices, with the first Brillouin zone shaded in red/pink around the central reciprocal lattice point in each case."}
:::
::::

---

## Brillouin zone

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Define a crystal lattice point by translating the objects by (integer multiples of) basis vectors, $\mathbf{a}$, and the corresponding reciprocal basis vectors, $\mathbf{b}$.

- Spatial lattice:
- $\mathbf{R}=n\mathbf{a}$, where $\mathbf{a}=a\hat{x}$ and $n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,...$
- Reciprocal lattice:
- $\mathbf{b}$ defined to satisfy $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}=2 \pi $, hence $\mathbf{b}=(2 \pi /a)\hat{x}$
- $\mathbf{K}=n\mathbf{B}$, where $n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,...$

- The first Brillouin zone corresponds to:

- $$k=0, \pm \frac{2 \pi }{Na}, \pm \frac{4 \pi }{Na},..., \pm \frac{(N-1) \pi }{Na},\frac{ \pi }{a}$$

- Bloch: any wave number $\mathbf{q}$ can be decomposed into a wave number $\mathbf{k}$ in the first Brillouin zone, and a wave number of the reciprocal lattice, $\mathbf{K}$.

---

## Bloch's theorem

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- A quick word on Bloch's theorem:

- Solutions to the Schroedinger equation in a periodic potential can be written as the product of a plane wave and a periodic function:
- $$ \psi (\mathbf{r})={e}^{i\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}} \cdot u(\mathbf{r})$$
- where $u(\mathbf{r})$ has the same periodicity as the potential (i.e. it's the same in every unit cell)

- Sketch proof: periodic potential can be written as Fourier transform,

- $$V(x)=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{K}{e}^{iKx}{V}_{K}$$

- Similarly, take Fourier transform of wave function, using the decomposability into a reciprocal lattice vector (K) and a wave vector in the 1st Brillouin zone (k):

- $$ \psi (x)=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{q}{e}^{iqx}{C}_{q}=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{K,k}{e}^{i(k+K)x}{C}_{k+K}$$

---

## Bloch's theorem

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Put this into the Schoedinger equation, $-\frac{{ \hbar }^{2}}{2m}\frac{{d}^{2} \psi }{d{x}^{2}}+V(x) \psi (x)=E \psi (x)$,

- $$\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k,K}\left\{ \left[ \frac{1}{2}(k+K{)}^{2}-E \right]{e}^{i(k+K)x}{C}_{k+K} \right\}+\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{L}{V}_{L}\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{K,k}{e}^{i(k+K+L)x}{C}_{k+K}=0$$

- (set ${ \hbar }^{2}/m=1$)

- We can redefine the summations to obtain:

- $$\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{K,k}{e}^{i(k+K)x}\left\{ \left[ \frac{1}{2}(k+K{)}^{2}-E \right]{C}_{k+K}+\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{L}{V}_{K-L}{C}_{k+L} \right\}=0$$

- Since the ${e}^{i(k+K)x}$ are linearly independent, the terms in ${}$ must each equal 0.
- Modes with different wave numbers, $k$, decouple.
  - ${ \psi }_{k}(x)={e}^{ikx}\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{K}{e}^{iKx}{c}_{k+K}={e}^{ikx}{u}_{k}(x)$, where ${u}_{k}(x+na)={u}_{k}(x)$.

---

## Bloch's theorem

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- So in short, our solutions take the form of a solution from the 1st Brillouin zone, modulated by a simple plane wave:

![Bloch_function.tiff](../assets/05_bvps/Bloch_function.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Sketch of a Bloch function: a rapidly oscillating periodic curve (solid) modulated by and bounded within a slowly-varying envelope (dashed), crossing a flat baseline."}

![BlochWaves1D.png](../assets/05_bvps/BlochWaves1D.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Six-panel grid illustrating the construction of a Bloch wave for two different k values (columns): the periodic part u(x) (top row), the plane-wave factor e^(ikx) (middle row), and their product, the full Bloch wave psi(x) = u(x)e^(ikx) (bottom row), each shown as overlaid real (blue) and imaginary (red) parts."}

---

## Band structure

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- To solve for the band structure, look at the eigenvalue equation:

- $$\left[ \frac{1}{2}(k+K{)}^{2}-E \right]{C}_{k+K}+\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{L}{V}_{K-L}{C}_{k+L}=0$$

- This is actually infinite-dimensional, so we cut if off somewhere.
- We look at the spectrum of states as a function of $k$, inside the first Brillouin zone. This is a "band."
  - In particular, let's find the relationship between $k$ and $E$.

---

## Band structure

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Concretely, look at a single cell on our lattice:

- $$V(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix}
0 & \text{for} & -\frac{a}{2}<x<-\frac{ \Delta }{2} \\
{V}_{0} & \text{for} & -\frac{ \Delta }{2}<x<\frac{ \Delta }{2} \\
0 & \text{for} & \frac{ \Delta }{2}<x<\frac{a}{2}
\end{matrix}\right.$$

- Between the barriers ($V=0$), we have solutions of form:

- $$ \psi (x)={A}_{n}{e}^{iq(x-na)}+{B}_{n}{e}^{-iq(x-na)}$$

- $$q=\sqrt{2E}$$

- Inside the barrier ($V={V}_{0}$), solution have form:

- $$ \psi (x)={C}_{n}{e}^{i \kappa (x-na)}+{D}_{n}{e}^{-i \kappa (x-na)}$$

- $$ \kappa =\sqrt{2(E-{V}_{0})}$$

- We determine ${A}_{n},{B}_{n},{C}_{n},{D}_{n}$ by matching $ \psi $ and ${ \psi }^{′}$ at the boundaries, resulting in a recursion relation:

- $$\left( \begin{aligned}
{A}_{n+1} \\
{B}_{n+1}
\end{aligned} \right)=\mathbf{T}(E)\left( \begin{aligned}
{A}_{n} \\
{B}_{n}
\end{aligned} \right)$$

---

## Band structure

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- The $T(E)$ is a "transfer matrix", with elements:

- $$\begin{matrix}
{T}_{11} & ={T}_{22}^{*}=\frac{{e}^{iq(a- \Delta )}}{4q \kappa }[{e}^{i \kappa  \Delta }(q+ \kappa {)}^{2}-{e}^{-i \kappa  \Delta }(q- \kappa {)}^{2}] \\
{T}_{12} & ={T}_{21}^{*}=-\frac{i{e}^{iq(a- \Delta )}}{2q \kappa }({q}^{2}-{ \kappa }^{2})sin( \kappa  \Delta )
\end{matrix}$$

- From Bloch's theorem, eigenvalues are of form ${e}^{ika}$, for $k$ = reduced wave number in the first Brillouin zone.
- $T(E)$ is just a $2 \times 2$ matrix, so it's easy to just solve $det[\mathbf{T}-{e}^{ika}\mathbf{1}]=0$.
- Result: quadratic equation with two solutions for $k(E)$, equal in magnitude, opposite in sign.
